---
title: "Standard deviation"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false

---

The [preceding page](variance-and-covariance.qmd) defined variance as an expected squared deviation from the mean. That squaring prevents cancellation, but it also changes the measurement units. How do we retain the spread information while returning to the original scale? We answer with the [CMUdict total phone counts](why-random-variables.qmd#the-pronunciation-entry-outcomes).

We take the square root of the phone-count variance, interpret the resulting distance in phones, and then show why one standard deviation does not by itself determine a fixed coverage probability.

```{r}
#| label: load-cmudict-sd
library(ggplot2)

cmu <- read.csv(
  "data/cmudict/cmudict-pronunciations.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = ""
)
phone_pmf <- as.data.frame(table(cmu$phone_count))
names(phone_pmf) <- c("phone_count", "entries")
phone_pmf$phone_count <- as.integer(as.character(phone_pmf$phone_count))
phone_pmf$mass <- phone_pmf$entries / nrow(cmu)

phone_mean <- mean(cmu$phone_count)
phone_variance <- mean((cmu$phone_count - phone_mean)^2)
phone_sd <- sqrt(phone_variance)
lower_one_sd <- phone_mean - phone_sd
upper_one_sd <- phone_mean + phone_sd
coverage_one_sd <- mean(
  cmu$phone_count >= lower_one_sd & cmu$phone_count <= upper_one_sd
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(cmu) == 133854L,
  phone_sd >= 0,
  abs(phone_sd^2 - phone_variance) < 1e-12,
  coverage_one_sd >= 0,
  coverage_one_sd <= 1
)

c(mean_phones = phone_mean,
  variance_phones_squared = phone_variance,
  standard_deviation_phones = phone_sd,
  empirical_coverage_within_one_sd = coverage_one_sd)
```

## Definition

The [**standard deviation**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) is the nonnegative square root of the variance:

$$
\sigma_X
\equiv
\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[X]}.
$$

For the empirical pronunciation-entry distribution,

$$
\widehat\sigma_X
=\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(X)}.
$$

The variance is `r sprintf("%.3f", phone_variance)` phones squared, and its square root is `r sprintf("%.3f", phone_sd)` phones. Taking the square root returns the spread summary to the measurement units of $X$.

```{r}
#| label: plot-cmudict-sd
#| fig-cap: "Empirical phone-count PMF. The blue line marks the mean; dashed lines mark one standard deviation on either side."
ggplot(phone_pmf, aes(phone_count, mass)) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightgrey", width = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = phone_mean, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(lower_one_sd, upper_one_sd),
    color = "grey", linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Phones in pronunciation", y = "Empirical probability") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## What standard deviation summarizes

Standard deviation is the square root of the expected squared distance from the mean. It is not the average absolute distance from the mean. Squaring gives greater weight to large deviations, so the two summaries need not agree.

The **mean absolute deviation** instead averages $|X-\mathbb{E}[X]|$ and thus
weights departures linearly. The [**standard error**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04) is a different object: it
is the standard deviation of an estimator's sampling distribution, such as
$\operatorname{sd}(\overline X)$. Standard deviation here describes variation
among pronunciation-entry counts, not uncertainty in an estimated parameter.

Standard deviation is also not a complete description of distribution shape. Equal means and standard deviations do not guarantee equal tails, symmetry, or modality.

## Standard deviation does not determine coverage

A fixed proportion of observations need not fall within one standard deviation of the mean. In this empirical PMF, `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * coverage_one_sd)` of pronunciation entries fall between `r sprintf("%.2f", lower_one_sd)` and `r sprintf("%.2f", upper_one_sd)` phones. The percentage is computed from CMUdict, not supplied by the definition of standard deviation.

Coverage statements require information about distribution shape. Until a particular family has been justified, standard deviation should be interpreted as a root mean squared distance, not as a guaranteed interval containing a fixed percentage of outcomes.

## Check your understanding

1. Compute the population standard deviation of `vowel_phone_count` and report its units.
2. Compare the empirical coverage within one standard deviation for total and vowel-phone counts.
3. Why do variance and standard deviation order two distributions by spread in the same way?
4. Which additional assumption would license a familiar normal-distribution coverage statement?
5. A student calls `phone_sd` the standard error of the mean. Which random
   variable does `phone_sd` actually summarize?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The population standard deviation of `vowel_phone_count` is $\sqrt{0.975784}=0.987818$ vowel phones. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Coverage within one standard deviation is 0.667615 for total phone count and 0.736609 for vowel-phone count. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Standard deviation is the strictly increasing square root of nonnegative variance, so comparing either summary gives the same ordering by spread. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. A normal-distribution assumption would license the familiar reference that about 68.27% of probability lies within one standard deviation of the mean. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. `phone_sd` summarizes the empirical distribution of raw pronunciation-entry
   phone counts $X$, not the sampling distribution of the estimator $\bar X$.

</details>

Standard deviation is the square root of variance and thus inherits its squared
weighting, unlike mean absolute deviation. It also should not be confused with
the standard error of an estimator. The [next page](central-moments.qmd)
changes the exponent to summarize other features of deviations from the mean.
